content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem's symptom, noting that account pages loaded slowly with no failures. The metric is median latency, and I'm now starting the causal chain, beginning with the slowdown itself and weighing whether to cite the alert label.

I'm checking the causal chain step by step: the cache connection refusals from 03:42 forced recomputation on each account page, the service was pointed at port 6380 by the config change, and that change came with deploy P2. I still need to rule out the earlier deploy P1 by confirming the service was healthy after it.

I'm checking the earlier deploy P1 against the metrics, which were read over the window from 23:42 to 03:43 and show the service healthy before the onset. I'm also noting that no flag changes happened in the hour before, and that the rollback to P1's revision recovered the service, which points at P2.

I'm settling the mechanism now: the deploy moved the cache address to port 6380, where the cache wasn't accepting connections, so every lookup was refused and each page fell back to recomputing the spend figure. That account rests on the connection-refused logs and the service's fallback behavior, not on any unverified reading of where the cache normally serves.

I'm lining up the chain's order now: the slowdown comes from pages recomputing the spend figure, which happened because every cache lookup was refused on port 6380, which in turn follows from the running config pointing at that port on every replica. The change that set that port was deploy P2, and it's the step that ties the incident to the rollout.

I'm now settling the final step of the chain: the change in deploy P2 set the cache port to one where the cache refused connections, which is what ties the incident to the rollout.

I'm settling the root cause: the deploy changed the cache port, so every lookup was refused and each account page recomputed the spend figure, which kept it correct but slow. I'm checking that a configuration change explains the incident in plain terms, with the mechanism resting on the logs and the service's fallback rather than on any unverified reading.

I'm now checking the closing advice: automatic sync should stay off until the repository's cache port is corrected, because the refused port is still set there and could reach production again and slow account pages.

I'm moving on to the contributing factors, starting with the missing check: nothing I've seen validates the cache address in deploy config before a rollout, so a wrong port could ship unnoticed.

I'm weighing the second contributing factor: the cache going unreachable degraded latency without any alert on connection failures, since the alert only fired on latency. I'm also considering whether a post-deploy gate that watches latency or cache errors and halts or rolls back would have caught this, and I'm checking that against the accounted window before I go further.

I'm weighing a third contributing factor: the HighLatency alert fired, but nobody was paged for it, so the incident went unattended by a person even though the alert itself worked.

I'm noting that the alert on latency was the only signal, so the cache's connection errors that started at 03:42 went unflagged. A rule on cache connection failures could have pointed straight at the cache and fired sooner than the latency rule's wait.

I'm turning to the action items: a pre-deploy check that the cache host and port accept connections, a progressive rollout that halts on rising latency or cache-lookup failures, an alert on those lookup failures, and routing the HighLatency alert to on-call paging. Then I'm starting the list of what went well, beginning with the investigator reading the D1 diff and Argus rolling back the deploy.

I'm noting the incident's open items: no one was paged for the latency alert, and the shop lost no takings while account pages stayed correct through the fallback. I'm holding the assumptions to check, since the cache accepting connections after rollback was inferred rather than measured, and the slow pages' cause rests on a code comment, not a profile.

I'm drafting the symptom step: account pages loaded slowly, with the median response time well above normal while failure counts stayed in range. I'm also checking that the series is the slowest replica's median, and noting that the cache-backed page recomputes each shopper's spend figure whenever it can't use the cache.

I'm settling the mechanism's details now: the port that the cache connection targets comes from the deploy config, and the cache refusing connections is what forces the fallback, so I'll tie the step to that config value and the replicas that run it. I'm also checking whether earlier deploy P1 could be the culprit, and I'm looking at the metrics to see whether the service was healthy with P1 in place before the onset.

I'm ruling out the earlier deploy P1 by checking that the service was healthy with it in place until the onset, and I'm ruling out flag changes since Argus was the only one touching flags in the hour before. I'm also ruling out a code change, since the deploy diff lists only the values file.

action_items.item: Add a pre-deploy check, in CI or at sync, that for every change to io-shop's deployment values confirms the configured cache host and port accept connections from the target environment, and blocks the deploy if they do not.
Roll io-shop deploys out progressively, with automated analysis that halts and rolls back the rollout when latency or summary-cache lookup failures rise on the first replicas.
Add an alert on io-shop summary-cache lookup failures (connection refused or unreachable).
Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly: the slowest replica's median time to answer a request rose far above its usual level, while failed requests stayed within their normal range.

Pages were slow because the account page could not use its rendered-summary cache. Its configuration says that when the cache cannot be reached, the page works out the shopper's spend figure from scratch, and the logs show that happening on every request.

The cache could not be used because every lookup was refused: the service connected to the cache on port {S1.3}, and the cache refused the connection. As read at {T14.1}, all replicas ran revision 0d8e826, whose configuration sets that port.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 544cef3 at {P1.1}: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset at {began}.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before {T17.4}.
A source-code change shipped in the same deploy: the diff lists only deploy/values-production.yaml, so every other file was as it was at the previous revision.

causal_chain.step: The service pointed at that port because the deploy of revision 0d8e826 at {P2.1} changed the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, a port on which the cache refused connections.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A configuration change gave the shop a cache address that refused its connections, so every account page had to be worked out from scratch: the pages stayed correct but got slow.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen, in review or before the deploy, that the cache address in the deployment configuration accepts connections. A change to the cache port shipped to production unchallenged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The refused port would have been caught before the deploy, and no account page would have slowed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The deploy reached every replica, and no gate was seen that watches latency or cache-lookup failures after rollout to halt or reverse it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The rollout would have stopped or reversed itself on the first replicas, before every shopper was served by the slow fallback.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No alert on summary-cache lookup failures was seen. The fault was found only by the latency alert, although connection-refused errors were logged from the first minute.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on cache lookup failures would have pointed straight at the cache and could have fired sooner than a latency rule that waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read what the deploy of revision 0d8e826 changed and found the cache port edit in the production values file.
Argus read the flag provider's history, which ruled out a flag change by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent rolled back the io-shop deployment off revision 0d8e826.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service after the rollback and judged the action confirmed.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix with a new test as draft pull request #551.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the HighLatency alert on io-shop was linked to no on-call incident.

input.root_cause: Revision 0d8e826 changed `cache.port` in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, and the summary cache refused connections on that port. Every summary-cache lookup failed, so on every request the account page fell back to working out each shopper's spend figure from scratch. That fallback keeps pages correct but slow.
input.still_at_risk: The refused cache port, or another wrong cache address, could reach production again and slow every account page.
